cues.text: A Soldier's Miraculous Escape

Born into a patrician Venetian family in 1481, Jerome served as a soldier for the Republic of Venice, and in 1508 was captured while defending the fortress of Castelnuovo against the League of Cambrai.
Held prisoner and chained, Jerome experienced what he understood as a miraculous liberation.
In fulfillment of a vow made during his captivity, he made a pilgrimage to the shrine of Our Lady at Treviso, leaving his prison chains there as an offering of thanksgiving.
From Magistrate to Priest

After a period serving as civil governor (podestà) of Castelnuovo, Jerome returned to Venice to oversee his orphaned nephews' upbringing, and devoted his spare time increasingly to theological study and works of charity.
Ordained a priest in 1518, he began spending his time in the hospitals and poorest quarters of Venice, tending to the sick and destitute.
Answering a Year of Plague and Famine
During the terrible year of plague and famine in 1528, Jerome threw himself entirely into relief work.
Contemporaries said he seemed to be everywhere at once, turning particular attention to the swelling numbers of orphaned children left behind by the crisis.
He rented a house near the church of St. Rose in Venice to shelter and care for these children directly.
A Growing Network of Charity
Jerome expanded his charitable work across northern Italy in the years that followed.
He induced Verona’s citizens to build a hospital and established orphanages for boys and girls at Bergamo.
He also established an orphanage at Brescia and founded what may have been the first refuge specifically for women seeking to leave prostitution.
He also took charge of a hospital for incurables that had been founded by St. Cajetan .
Founding the Somaschi
In 1532, joined by two fellow priests, Jerome formally founded a religious congregation dedicated to the care of orphans, the poor, and the sick.
He established its motherhouse at the secluded hamlet of Somasca between Milan and Bergamo, the origin of the order later known as the Somaschi Fathers.
Their rule insisted that the community's dwellings, food, and clothing all bear the visible mark of genuine religious poverty.
Legacy
Jerome died at Somasca in 1537, reportedly of a fever contracted while nursing the sick, and was canonized in 1767 by Pope Clement XIII.

In 1928, Pope Pius XI named him the universal patron of orphans and abandoned children, a fitting recognition for a former soldier whose own miraculous escape from captivity redirected an entire life toward rescuing society's most vulnerable.
